summary: This informational document specifies how to carry Kerberos V5 over TLS for extra security features. The Kerberos messages travel through a TLS connection. It is not a standard.

eli5.summary: Kerberos is a ticket system for proving who you are. This puts its messages inside a protected tunnel so others can't peek or tamper.

questions: what is the kerberos-tls srv record
subtitle: How a Kerberos client and its KDC can upgrade their TCP connection to TLS for privacy and extra authentication.

tldr.problem: Parts of Kerberos V5 messages travel without integrity or privacy protection, so an active attacker can tamper with encryption type or pre-authentication choices, and observers can read names and ticket details.
tldr.mechanism: The client sets the STARTTLS bit in the Kerberos V5 TCP extension mechanism, the server answers with 0x00000000, and a TLS handshake follows. The normal Kerberos exchange then runs inside the TLS channel.
tldr.outcome: TLS guards against downgrade attacks and passive sniffing, and can add authentication of the KDC. Clients are not required to verify server certificates, which leaves room for man-in-the-middle attacks unless they do.

facts.label: Extension bit
facts.value: Bit 0 in the Kerberos TCP extension bitmask

facts.label: Server certificate check
facts.value: Not required, MUST if client is able

today: RFC 6251 is an Informational document, published in May 2011. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Run Kerberos over TLS
sections.content:
This document describes how a Kerberos V5 implementation may upgrade communication between clients and Key Distribution Centers (KDCs) to use Transport Layer Security (TLS). TLS offers integrity- and privacy-protected exchanges that can be authenticated with X.509 certificates, OpenPGP keys, or usernames and passwords via SRP.

The RFC gives four reasons. It prevents downgrade attacks: the encryption type in KDC-REQ and the pre-auth list in KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED errors are sent unprotected in plain Kerberos V5, so an active attacker could swap in a weak type such as 56-bit DES. It makes exchanges private, hiding principal names, supported encryption types and ticket lifetimes. It adds authentication against the KDC, for example with smart cards or OpenPGP keys. And it gives the client explicit authentication of the KDC, where plain Kerberos only proves it as a side effect of the KDC knowing the user's key.
sections.eli5: Normally some of the notes Kerberos passes around are written on the outside of the envelope. TLS puts the whole thing in a locked box, so no one can read or change them.

sections.title: The STARTTLS Extension
sections.content:
The extension builds on the Kerberos V5 TCP extension mechanism from RFC 5021 and uses bit 0 of the extension bitmask. The client asks for it by setting the STARTTLS bit. When the server has sent the 4-octet value 0x00000000 to show it supports the extension, the stream is controlled by TLS and its framing, and the client starts the handshake.

If the handshake fails, the STARTTLS protocol fails too, the TLS error is the error indication, and no more messages can be exchanged on that TCP session. If it succeeds, the Kerberos exchange runs inside the TLS channel like a normal TCP Kerberos exchange, so every Kerberos packet is still prefixed by a 4-octet length field.

When no more Kerberos messages need to be sent, the TLS session MUST be shut down with the close_notify alert. The TCP connection then cannot be reused and MUST be closed.
sections.eli5: The client knocks and asks, 'can we talk in a sealed tube?' If the server says yes, they set up the tube first and only then start the real conversation. When they are done they close the tube and hang up.

sections.title: A Complete Packet Flow
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a successful AS-REQ/AS-REP exchange. First the extension negotiation happens in the clear: the client sends 0x80000000 ORed with the STARTTLS bit and the server replies 0x00000000.

Then the TLS handshake runs, from ClientHello to the Finished messages, with some messages (such as Certificate and CertificateRequest) marked as optional or situation-dependent. Only after that does the client send a length field and the Kerberos AS-REQ, and the server answer with a length field and the AS-REP, all inside TLS.
sections.eli5: First they agree to use the tube. Then they set up the tube. Only then does the client ask for its ticket and get it back, safely inside.

sections.title: Finding a STARTTLS-Aware KDC
sections.content:
Kerberos V5 already uses DNS SRV records to find KDCs. This RFC defines a new service name, kerberos-tls, to show that a given KDC is meant to support the STARTTLS extension. The Proto (tcp), Realm, TTL, Class, SRV, Priority, Weight, Port and Target fields mean the same as in RFC 4120.

The RFC's example publishes two records for EXAMPLE.COM, _kerberos-tls._tcp.EXAMPLE.COM., pointing at kdc1.example.com. (priority 0) and kdc2.example.com. (priority 1), both on port 88.
sections.eli5: It is a phone book entry that says which Kerberos servers can use the sealed tube, so clients know where to call.

sections.title: Server Certificates
sections.content:
A stated goal is that this protocol should be as easy to implement and deploy on clients as UDP/TCP support. Many clients have no long-term storage secure enough to validate server certificates, so the extension does not require clients to verify server certificates. The RFC argues that TLS even without validation still protects against passive sniffing aimed at tracking a client's Kerberos service use, but it warns that active attacks such as man in the middle become possible.

When clients have the ability, they MUST validate the server certificate. If a KDC presents an X.509 certificate, it MUST contain an otherName Subject Alternative Name identified by id-krb5starttls-san, whose value is the Kerberos realm. Clients MAY instead use local configuration, such as a list mapping realms to server certificates, or MAY use certification path validation from RFC 5280. Unless the client can otherwise verify that the certificate is bound to the target realm's KDC, it MUST check that the SAN is present and equals the intended realm.
sections.eli5: Checking the server's ID card is the best idea, but some small devices cannot keep a list of trusted cards. So checking is only a must for clients that are able to do it.

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of Kerberos V5, TLS and the Kerberos V5 TCP extension mechanism are inherited. TLS does not protect against man-in-the-middle attacks unless clients verify the KDC's credentials correctly. If server authentication is used, some information about the server, such as its name, is visible to passive attackers.

To protect against the downgrade attack inherent in the extension framework, implementations SHOULD offer a policy mode that requires the extension to be negotiated successfully for a particular realm or generally. That mode SHOULD be disabled by default for interoperability with implementations that lack the extension.

IANA allocated bit value 0 in the Kerberos TCP Extensions registry for this extension.
sections.eli5: If you only ever say 'tube if possible', a trickster can talk you out of using it. So there should be a switch that insists on the tube, though it starts switched off so old servers still work.
